Daylight

daylight is the sun's clock for appearance.mode = auto. It works out the next sunrise or sunset for where the machine is and, when one passes, writes state.appearance.daylight into settingsd. settingsd's resolver turns auto into light or dark from that key, so every desk, app and desktop exporter follows the change by the normal path: one revision, one receipt.

  • Where. The place comes from time.zone. While that key is unset, it comes from the zone the host's /etc/localtime names. A table in <prefix>/share/daylight/zones.mx gives each zone its principal place, the city the IANA time zone database names it after (tzdb chooses the region's most populous city). There is no GPS, no network lookup and no user-set location. A zone with no place (UTC, Etc/GMT+10) gives the sun as unknown (null), and auto then resolves to dark.
  • When. The standard sunrise equation, with the sun's centre at 0.833 degrees below the horizon, which allows for refraction and the solar disc. It is within a minute or two of published times away from the poles. Inside the polar circles, a polar day is light and a polar night is dark; the day a polar day or night begins, the change is taken at that day's solar midnight, so the state still alternates sunrise, sunset across the boundary. The next event daylight waits for is always the one that changes the state: a sunset while it is light, a sunrise while it is dark.
  • A manual flip holds until the next event. Choosing Light or Dark while the mode is auto sets state.appearance.mode_override. daylight clears it in the same revision that next changes state.appearance.daylight, so the override lasts until the next sunrise or sunset. A zone change that changes the sun's state clears it the same way, including a change to a zone with no place (daylight becomes null).

Until daylight has written its key, Preferences shows the Auto choice disabled, naming daylight.mix.

Running it

daylight runs once per machine, beside the settings authority, never beside a mirror: a desk's mirror relays the authority's revisions, so every desk on the machine flips together. Before its first write it asks settings.status; beside a mirror (any role but authority) it logs why and exits 0, writing nothing. It is a Mix Bus citizen; the user unit runs it in the authority's session:

$ systemctl --user enable --now mixos-daylight.service

The unit is installed as <prefix>/share/daylight/units/daylight.service; copy or link it into ~/.config/systemd/user/ as mixos-daylight.service.

It binds {instance: <node>, profile: "default"}, the node being the native node identity (MIXOS_NODE_CONFIG). The environment can change that and the rest:

VariableDefaultWhat
MIXOS_DAYLIGHT_INSTANCEthe node namethe settings instance
MIXOS_DAYLIGHT_SETTINGSDsettingsdthe settingsd service to call
MIXOS_DAYLIGHT_ZONES<share>/daylight/zones.mxthe zone table
MIXOS_DAYLIGHT_LOCALTIME/etc/localtimethe link that names the host's zone
MIXOS_DAYLIGHT_RESUMEonoff stops the login1 watch

Nothing polls

daylight arms one local timer, for the next sunrise or sunset, and works the sun out again only when something changes:

  • at start, and on each broker connection;
  • on every revision of the time keys (the retained settingsd.desktop.keys.default.time topic), taken only for its own binding and only when the revision is newer than the last one seen;
  • when the timer fires;
  • when /etc/localtime is replaced (an inotify watch on its directory);
  • on resume from suspend: logind's PrepareForSleep(false) signal, heard through gdbus monitor on the system bus. The timer runs on the monotonic clock, which stops during suspend, so resume is when it must be re-armed. If the watch exits, it is restarted, at most once a minute.

When no sunrise or sunset falls in the four solar days it looks at (a long polar day or night), or the zone has no place, it looks again in a day.

It writes only when the sun's state differs from the stored one, fenced on the revision it read; when another commit lands in between it reads again, up to three times.

Mix has no way to cancel a sleeping task, so one wake task does the waiting: a later deadline is taken up by the task already sleeping when it wakes, and only an earlier one starts a new task (the old one finds itself superseded and ends).

Commands

CommandAnswers
daylight.status{binding, role, zone, zone_from, place, daylight, next, next_kind, due, tasks_started, writes, last_reason, last_error, resume, resumes, resume_restarts, localtime_watch, clock_offset}: zone_from is time.zone or localtime; next the Unix time of the next event and due the armed wake; resume is login1, restarting, unavailable, lost or off; clock_offset is 0 outside tests
$ mix -c 'send daylight daylight.status; print($result)'

Limits

  • A wall-clock step (an NTP correction at boot, a manual clock change) is not heard: the timer then fires late or early by the step. A late timer still writes the right state when it fires, and an early one finds nothing to change and re-arms.
  • Where a desk has no system bus, or no gdbus, resume is not heard and the first event after a resume is late by the time spent suspended. daylight.status reports it as resume: "unavailable".

Testing

services/daylight/tests/daylight_test.mix runs the maths, the zone table, the citizen against a real settingsd on a private Bus, and against a fake one (tests/fixtures/fake_settingsd.mix) for a mirror's role and for conflicts. With MIXOS_TEST=1 only, the citizen honours three test hooks: MIXOS_DAYLIGHT_CLOCK_OFFSET (seconds added to the wall clock; it must be a number and is clamped to seven days either way), MIXOS_DAYLIGHT_RESUME_ARGV (a JSON argv run instead of gdbus monitor) and MIXOS_DAYLIGHT_RESUME_GUARD (seconds between watch restarts).

The zone table

share/daylight/zones.mx is generated, not written by hand:

$ mix services/daylight/tools/zones_from_tzdb.mix [--tzdata /usr/share/zoneinfo] [--check]

It takes each zone's coordinates from tzdb's zone.tab (one row per country and zone), then zone1970.tab for any zone that lacks them, then gives every tzdata.zi link (such as Australia/Queensland) its target's place, repeating until no link gains one. The time zone database is in the public domain; its licence is in share/daylight/LICENSE-tzdb.txt and LICENSES/LicenseRef-Public-Domain.txt, and the table is listed in tools/assets.conf.mix.
